passages.title: Oaths as a shield: the hypocrites unmasked
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat open a sūrah that is, from beginning to end, about a specific kind of person: the one who says the right words and means none of them. They come to the Prophet ﷺ with a declaration of faith on their lips, and Allah answers not by denying what they said but by exposing what lies behind it.

## The moment behind the revelation

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the occasion in unusual detail.

The setting is the campaign against Banū al-Muṣṭaliq — dated by Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq to Shaʿbān 6 AH, and by Qatādah and ʿUrwah to Shaʿbān 5 AH (cited via Mazharī). Word reached the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that Ḥārith ibn Ḍirār, the leader of Banū al-Muṣṭaliq, was preparing to move against him, so he gathered a body of Muslims and went out. The armies met near a well called Muraysīʿ — hence the campaign's other name. Arrows were exchanged, many of Banū al-Muṣṭaliq were killed and others fled, men and women were taken captive, and some of their belongings fell to the Muslims as spoils. Allah granted victory to the Prophet ﷺ.

**Many hypocrites had joined this expedition** — not out of faith, but because, holding disbelief in their hearts, they were nonetheless sure that divine help would be on the Prophet's ﷺ side and that he would attain victory. They came in the hope of a share in the spoils. They could see that he would be helped, and still they would not believe.

**The quarrel at the well.** While the army was still at Muraysīʿ, an emigrant (Muhājir) and a helper (Anṣārī) fell into a dispute over the same water where the battle had been fought. Each man called out to his own faction for help, individuals came forward to take sides, and it could have led to a fight between the Muhājirūn and the Anṣār. The Prophet ﷺ came straight to the scene and expressed his indignation: *"What is this slogan of paganism?"* — the call to rally on the basis of regional, racial and national bias — and, *"Give up the slogan. It stinks."* He taught that a Muslim helps his brother whether that brother is the oppressed or the oppressor: helping the oppressed is obvious; helping the oppressor means stopping him from oppression. The two men were Jahjāh the emigrant, who was more in the wrong, and Sinān ibn Wabrah al-Juhanī the helper, who was wounded. Sayyidnā ʿUbādah ibn Ṣāmit intervened between them, and oppressor and oppressed became brothers.

**ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy's speech.** The leader of the hypocrites saw the friction and found in it an ideal opportunity. Addressing a gathering that included the Companion Zayd ibn Arqam, he provoked the Anṣār with a fiery speech against the emigrants: you let them settle in your land and share your wealth, they were fed on your bread until they grew strong and now they rival you; stop helping them and they will disperse. Then the line the sūrah answers: *"By Allah, when we go back to Madīnah the most honourable of the inhabitants of Madīnah shall drive out the meanest of them from there"* — by "the honourable" meaning his own group and the Anṣār, and by "the meanest" the Prophet ﷺ along with the Muhājirūn. Zayd ibn Arqam retorted instantly: *"By Allah, you are mean, low and despicable. The Messenger of Allah is successful by the honour Allah has given him, and by the love of the Muslims."*

Notice how Ibn Ubayy had spoken: under cover of a vague expression — "the most honoured," "the meanest" — naming no one. That was deliberate; he wanted to keep his hypocrisy under a veil. When Zayd's sharp retort showed him that his disbelief was about to be uncovered, he apologised to Zayd, saying he was merely joking and meant nothing against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

**The oath.** Zayd went and reported the whole story. The news was disturbing and trying for the Prophet ﷺ; the colour of his blessed countenance changed. Zayd was a young Companion at the time, and the Prophet ﷺ asked him, "Boy! Are you not perhaps lying?" — and Zayd made the same reply. The report spread through the whole army until no one spoke of anything else; the Anṣār reproached him for accusing the venerable leader of his people and severing kinship ties. Zayd swore by Allah that in the entire tribe of Khazraj no one was dearer to him than Ibn Ubayy, but that he could not hold himself when those words were uttered against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — "even if that were my father, I would have certainly reported his speech to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ."

Sayyidnā ʿUmar asked permission to behead the hypocrite. The Prophet ﷺ said that if he permitted it, the news would spread among people that Muḥammad ﷺ kills his own comrades — and so he did not allow it. When Ibn Ubayy's son — also named ʿAbdullāh, and a sincere Muslim — heard of ʿUmar's request, he came and offered to carry out the execution himself and bring the head before the Prophet ﷺ rose from his assembly, explaining that the whole of Khazraj could witness that no one served and obeyed his parents more than he did, but that he would not tolerate their mischief against Allah and His Messenger ﷺ; his fear was that if another man killed his father, tribal jealousy might overcome him and he would be tempted to kill the killer, and that might be the cause of his own punishment. The Prophet ﷺ replied: *"I do not have the intention of killing him, nor have I instructed anyone else to kill him."*

Then, at an unusual time and against his normal habit, the Prophet ﷺ announced an immediate departure for Madīnah. When the Companions had set out, he called Ibn Ubayy and asked him plainly: did you say this? **Ibn Ubayy took an oath and denied everything**, and claimed that the boy Zayd was a liar. He was the respectable chief of his people; the people felt that Zayd must have been under some misconception. The Prophet ﷺ accepted his oath and his explanation — and the reproach against Zayd was further aggravated, until the young man hid himself from people. The army travelled the whole day and night and the next morning until the bright sun was out, and when they finally halted, exhausted by the long and strenuous journey, they fell into deep sleep as soon as they touched the ground. The narrator reports that the purpose of that unusually immediate and long march was precisely to close the chapter of Ibn Ubayy's story.

Later on that journey, ʿUbādah ibn Ṣāmit suggested to Ibn Ubayy that he approach the Prophet ﷺ and admit his guilt, and the Prophet ﷺ would pray to Allah for his pardon and he would attain salvation. Ibn Ubayy turned his head away. Until that moment no verses had been revealed concerning him; when he turned away in haughty arrogance, ʿUbādah said, "Certainly, the Qurʼān will reveal verses pertaining to your turning down the advice."

**The vindication.** Zayd kept coming near the Prophet ﷺ, firm in the conviction that since the hypocrite had called him a liar and embarrassed him before the whole nation, Allah would surely reveal verses to clear him and give the lie to the hypocrite. Then he noticed the Prophet ﷺ entering the state he experienced when revelation came — breathing heavily, his forehead dripping with perspiration, his she-camel beginning to feel the weight of it. When that state was over, the Prophet ﷺ — Zayd's mount being nearest — took hold of the boy's ear and said: *"O Boy, Allah has confirmed the veracity of your statement, and the entire Sūrah al-Munāfiqūn — from the beginning to the end — has been revealed in connection with Ibn Ubayy's incident."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes a variant from Baghawī, that the Prophet ﷺ had already reached Madīnah and Zayd was hiding in his house for fear of reprisal when the sūrah was revealed — "and Allah knows best."

By another narration, as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ approached Madīnah at the valley of ʿAqīq, Ibn Ubayy's believing son searched through the throng of mounts, found his father's, made it sit, put his foot on its knees and told his father he could not enter Madīnah until the Messenger of Allah ﷺ permitted him and until he made clear who was the most honourable — the Messenger of Allah ﷺ or himself. Passers-by reproached the son for treating his father so unkindly. Ibn Ubayy declared that he himself was the meanest of the citizens of Madīnah, meaner than the children and the women, and that the Prophet ﷺ was the most honourable of them. Then the Prophet ﷺ came near and said, "Leave his way; let him enter."

## Words that are true, and a witness that is false

Read ayah 1 against that scene and it becomes almost physical. They say, *"We bear witness that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah."* Allah then confirms the content of their statement — *"Allah knows that you are indeed His Messenger"* — and only after that declares, *"and Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are liars indeed."*

Ibn Kathīr draws out the point with care. When the hypocrites come to the Prophet ﷺ, they announce this statement and pretend to believe in it — and Allah informs us that there is no substance to their statement. Their claim is false even though what they said about the Prophet ﷺ is true, because they did not believe inwardly in what they declared outwardly; and this is why Allah declared their falsehood about their creed.

A true sentence can carry no truth at all in the mouth of the one saying it, because the sentence is not merely a report; it is a claim about the speaker's own heart. And notice the two divine acts set side by side in the ayah: Allah *knows*, and Allah *bears witness*. Their testimony had nothing behind it; the testimony that settles the matter is His.

That is why the very next ayah turns to their oaths: *"They have made their oaths a screen. Thus they hinder others from the path of Allah."* Ibn Ubayy's defence, in the story, was exactly this — an oath sworn to deny his own words and to brand a truthful boy a liar. The word rendered here as "a screen," and elsewhere as "a shield," is explained by Ibn Kathīr in just that sense: the hypocrites shield themselves from the Muslims when they falsely and sinfully swear to be what they are not in reality.

Ibn Kathīr spells out how a mere oath does so much damage: some Muslims were deceived because they did not know the falsehood, and so thought that these men were Muslims; some believed what the hypocrites said and even imitated them in their outward behaviour. But inwardly these men sought the destruction of Islam and its people — which is why trusting them might bring great harm to many. That is why the ayah closes on *"evil is what they used to do."* The lie is not a private sin; it bends the community's judgement. In this very story, one oath was enough to make a whole army doubt an honest young Companion.

## The sealed heart, and the shape it leaves behind

Ayah 3 gives the cause: *"That is because they believed, and then disbelieved; therefore their hearts are sealed, so they understand not."* Ibn Kathīr explains: Allah decreed them to be hypocrites because they reverted from faith to disbelief and exchanged guidance for misguidance; therefore He stamped and sealed their hearts, and because of that they cannot comprehend the guidance, nor can any goodness reach their hearts — truly, their hearts neither understand nor attain guidance.

The order in the ayah is the order of the reality: the turning away comes first, the sealing follows it. Ibn Ubayy called himself a Muslim for worldly benefit while concealing enmity in his heart against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the Muslims; the hypocrites marched out on this very campaign while sure that divine help would be on the Prophet's ﷺ side. They could calculate that he would win. Not one thing of it reached their hearts.

Ayah 4 shows what the same men look like from the outside. *"And when you look at them, their bodies please you; and when they speak, you listen to their words."* Ibn Kathīr: the hypocrites have a graceful outer appearance and are eloquent; when a person hears them speak he will listen to their eloquent words — even though they are truly weak and feeble, full of fear, fright and cowardice. Then the Qurʼān's own image: *"They are as blocks of wood propped up."* Ibn Kathīr: they are shapes that do not have much substance.

*"They think that every cry is against them."* Ibn Kathīr reads this as their cowardice: every time an incident occurs or something frightening happens, they think it is headed their way. He connects it with Allah's description elsewhere of those who, when fear comes, look at you with their eyes revolving like one over whom death hovers, and when the fear departs smite you with sharp tongues (33:19). Fine bodies and fine speech, and underneath, nothing to stand on.

*"They are the enemies, so beware of them. May Allah curse them!"* And the closing question, which Ibn Kathīr glosses as: how are they being led astray to misguidance, away from the guidance?

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathīr cites here a narration recorded by Imam Aḥmad from Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said the hypocrites have certain signs by which they are known: their greeting is really a curse; their food is from stealing and the war booty they collect is from theft; they shun the Masjid and do not come to the prayer except at its end; they are arrogant, so that it is neither easy for them to blend in nor easy for people to blend with them; **they are like pieces of wood by night and are noisy by day.** The same word for wood that the ayah uses appears again in that description.

## Living it

**Truthfulness that costs you something.** Zayd ibn Arqam was young; Ibn Ubayy was the leader of his tribe and, as Zayd swore, the dearest person in all of Khazraj to him. He spoke anyway, and bore his own people's reproach for it — "even if that were my father." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān holds this up as an eloquent testimony to how deeply faith had settled in the Companions: they had such love and reverence for Allah and His Messenger ﷺ that no relationship and no sense of nationality could act as a barrier against it — and it adds the sting that the tribe-worshippers of the present age would never have dared carry such a complaint against their own leaders. Ibn Ubayy's own son showed the same thing from the other side: the most serving and obedient of sons, who would not let his father into Madīnah until he admitted the truth, and who would not open the way for him without the Prophet's ﷺ permission.

**The stinking slogan.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the quarrel at the well a foundational lesson: calling for help on the basis of tribe, race, language or region was the icon of paganism that the Prophet ﷺ destroyed, naming it a slogan that stinks. He re-established the community on the Qurʼānic principle, *"And help each other in righteousness and piety, and do not help each other in sin and aggression"* (5:2) — so the standard for whom you help, and from whom you accept help, is good will, justice, fair play and equity, even when the other person belongs to another race, ethnic group or region; and you do not unite with someone in sin and injustice even if he is your father or your brother. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the sobering observation that the enemies of Islam have used nationalism and regionalism to fracture the Muslim community since time immemorial.

**Guarding the community from misunderstanding.** When ʿUmar asked to behead Ibn Ubayy, the Prophet ﷺ declined so that it would not be said that Muḥammad ﷺ kills his own comrades. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān derives a principle from this: an act permissible in itself should be avoided if doing it may create a misunderstanding in a Muslim's mind, or give the enemies an opening to spread one. But it adds an important limit — as other traditions prove, such acts may be set aside only when they are not among the basic objectives of the Sharīʿah; those cannot be abandoned out of such apprehension. There, the effort must go into removing the danger while still doing what the objectives of the Sharīʿah require.

**And a word about the door left open.** ʿUbādah ibn Ṣāmit went to Ibn Ubayy and told him plainly: go to the Prophet ﷺ, admit your guilt, let him pray to Allah for your pardon, and you will attain salvation. It was haughty arrogance that turned his head away — and only then did the verses come down. The same campaign that produced these ayat also produced Juwayriyah bint al-Ḥārith, a captive under a contract of freedom she could not pay, who came to the Prophet ﷺ and said that she had embraced Islam and bore witness that there is only One Allah with no partners and that he is Allah's Messenger — the very words the hypocrites were mouthing without meaning. She became one of the noble wives of the Prophet ﷺ, and about a hundred captives of her people were emancipated on her account; her own father, the man who had marched out to fight, saw a miracle of the Prophet ﷺ and embraced Islam. The words are the same words. Everything depends on what stands behind them.

passages.title: Pride in Medina, and who truly holds honour
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat put us inside a real crisis in Madinah. A door of mercy is held open to the hypocrites and they turn their faces from it (ayah 5); Allah then closes it (ayah 6); and we are shown the two weapons they reached for instead — starving the believers of money (ayah 7) and stirring up tribal pride to drive them out of the city (ayah 8). What holds the passage together is a single word: honour. The hypocrites thought honour was something they possessed and could withhold. The passage ends by telling them where honour actually lives.

## The offer they refused

Ibn Kathir reports that several of the Salaf (the earliest generations) said this whole passage came down concerning one man: 'Abdullah bin Ubay bin Salul, the chief of the hypocrites of Madinah.

Ibn Ishaq records in his *Sirah* a scene from just after the battle of Uhud. Ibn Ubay had a standing privilege: every Friday, as the Prophet ﷺ sat on the minbar before the khutbah, Ibn Ubay would rise — no one objected, because he was a chief of his people — and say, "O people! This is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with you. Allah has honoured us by sending him and gave you might through him. Support him, honour him and listen to and obey him." Then he would sit. After Uhud — after he had turned back to Madinah with a third of the army — he stood to say the same words, and this time the Muslims took hold of his clothes: "Sit down, O enemy of Allah! You are not worthy to stand after you did what you did." He pushed out through the rows muttering that he had only meant to support him. At the gate of the masjid some men of the Ansar met him and heard his complaint, and they gave him the advice that ayah 5 quotes: "Woe to you! Go back so that Allah's Messenger ﷺ asks Allah to forgive you." His answer was: "By Allah, I do not wish that he ask Allah to forgive me."

Read ayah 5 again with that sentence ringing in your ears. **Come — the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you.** This is not a demand for money or for war. It is an offer that the most beloved of Allah's creation will stand and beg his Lord on your behalf. And a man says: I would rather not.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places the same refusal at the moment this surah exposed his false oaths. People went to him and urged him: there is still time, go to the Prophet ﷺ, admit his guilt, ask him to pray to Allah to forgive him. He turned his head around and said arrogantly: I believed when you asked me to believe, I paid Zakah when you asked me to, and now the only thing left is for you to ask me to prostrate to Muhammad ﷺ. Maʿārif comments that these ayat were revealed on that occasion and make plain that he had no faith — which is precisely why asking forgiveness for him could not benefit him in any way. Maʿārif adds, on the authority of Mazhari, that after this incident Ibn Ubay returned to Madinah, lived for a few days, and died soon thereafter.

Qatadah and As-Suddi give a third angle: a young relative of Ibn Ubay carried an ugly statement of his to the Messenger ﷺ; Ibn Ubay was summoned and swore by Allah that he had said nothing; the Ansar went to that boy and admonished him — and then the revelation came down about Ibn Ubay's case. He was told, "Go to Allah's Messenger," and he turned his head away and said he would not do it.

## "They twist their heads"

The Arabic of ayah 5 is a picture, not an abstraction: **lawwaw ru'ūsahum** — they twist, they wrench their heads round. Ibn Kathir explains it as turning away, ignoring the call in arrogance and belittling what they are being invited to. It is body language everyone recognises — the shoulder that turns, the chin that lifts, the refusal that never has to be spoken.

And then the ayah adds the eye-witness clause: **and you would see them turning away their faces in pride** (*mustakbirūn*) — the very arrogance Ibn Kathir identifies, which belittles what it is being invited to. The Qur'an is not guessing at their hearts. It is describing a scene the Prophet ﷺ could watch happening in front of him. Arrogance is exactly what makes forgiveness impossible to receive: the one thing an offer of mercy requires is the willingness to be someone who needs it.

## Why ayah 6 shuts the door

Ayah 6 is Allah's response to that behaviour — Ibn Kathir says plainly that Allah punished them for it with these words: **It is equal to them whether you ask forgiveness or ask not forgiveness for them, Allah will never forgive them.**

This needs care, because it is easy to misread. The Prophet's ﷺ prayer is not being called weak. The point is that a prayer for forgiveness reaches a heart that has faith in it; here there was no faith to reach, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says. Ibn Kathir notes that Allah said the like of this in Surat Bara'ah, where a discussion of the matter preceded.

The ayah closes with the reason: **Verily, Allah guides not the people who are the rebellious** — *al-fāsiqīn*, those who have broken out of obedience and gone on breaking out. Notice the sequence: not "Allah refuses to guide, so they rebelled", but that persistent, chosen rebellion is what the withholding of guidance follows. The door was open in ayah 5. They twisted their heads away from it. Ayah 6 tells them what that costs.

## Ayah 7: the boycott, and who really feeds whom

**They are the ones who say: "Spend not on those who are with Allah's Messenger, until they desert him."** This was a strategy. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the ayah points to the foolish statement Ibn Ubay made at the time of the dispute between Jahjah the Emigrant and Sinan the Helper (the incident detailed below): cut off the money, and those who are with the Messenger ﷺ will disperse on their own. No swords needed.

Allah's answer does not argue with the tactic; it dissolves the assumption underneath it: **And to Allah belong the treasures of the heavens and the earth.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws it out: these foolish people presumed that the Emigrants needed their donations and that they were the ones sustaining them — while all the treasures of the heavens and the earth belong to Allah, and if He wills He can provide them everything without any contribution from anyone's side.

That is why the ayah ends **but the hypocrites comprehend not** — *lā yafqahūn*. Hold onto that word; ayah 8 will end with a different one, and the difference is deliberate.

**Living it:** this is the ayah for anyone who has ever been made to feel that their livelihood is a leash. The believer's provision passes through people's hands, but it does not originate there. Whoever thinks he is your provider has misunderstood the universe. And the mirror image is a warning: never imagine that what you give to a good cause is what keeps it alive. The treasuries are not yours.

## Ayah 8: the sentence that named the wrong man

Now the sirah that ayah 8 quotes. Ibn Ishaq's teachers — Muhammad bin Yahya bin Hibban, 'Abdullah bin Abi Bakr and 'Asim bin 'Umar bin Qatadah — related the story of Bani Al-Mustaliq. While the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was in that area, a fight broke out over the water source between Jahjah bin Sa'id Al-Ghifari, a hired hand of 'Umar, and Sinan bin Wabr. Sinan called out "O Ansar!" and Jahjah called "O Muhajirin!" — the old tribal war-cries, suddenly alive again.

Zayd bin Arqam, then a young boy, was sitting with 'Abdullah bin Ubay and several men of the Ansar when the news came. Ibn Ubay said: "They are bothering us in our land. By Allah, the parable of us and these foolish Quraysh men is the parable that goes, 'Feed your dog until it becomes strong, and it will eat you.' By Allah, when we go back to Al-Madinah, the most mighty will expel the weak from it." Then he turned on his own people: "What have you done to yourselves? You let them settle in your land and shared your wealth with them. By Allah, if you abandon them, they will have to move to another area other than yours." There is ayah 7 and ayah 8 in one speech — the boycott and the expulsion.

Zayd carried it to the Messenger ﷺ. 'Umar bin Al-Khattab was sitting there and said, "O Allah's Messenger! Order 'Abbad bin Bishr to cut off his head at his neck." The Prophet ﷺ replied: **"What if people started saying that Muhammad kills his companions, O 'Umar? No. However, order the people to start the journey."** Ibn Ubay came and swore by Allah that he had never uttered the statement Zayd conveyed — and because he was a chief of his people, they offered him cover: perhaps the young boy merely guessed and did not hear correctly. The Messenger ﷺ set out at an unusual hour of the day, and Usayd bin Al-Hudayr met him, greeted him acknowledging his prophethood, and remarked on the strange timing. The Prophet ﷺ said, "Did not the statement of your friend, Ibn Ubay reach you? He claimed that when he returns to Al-Madinah, the mighty one will expel the weak one out of it." Usayd answered: "Indeed, you are the mighty one, O Allah's Messenger, and he is the disgraced one." Then he added something that explains everything: "Take it easy with him, O Allah's Messenger! By Allah, when Allah brought you to us, we were about to gather the pearls (of a crown) so that we appoint him king over us. He thinks that you have rid him of his kingship."

That is the whole disease in one line. He had been days away from a crown. This passage is the sound of a man mourning a throne he never got.

The Prophet ﷺ then travelled with the people until night fell, then the rest of the night until the beginning of the next day, and only then set camp — because he wanted to keep them too occupied to talk about what had happened. The minute people felt the ground under their feet they went to sleep. And Surat Al-Munafiqin was revealed.

Al-Hafiz Abu Bakr Al-Bayhaqi records a parallel report from Jabir bin 'Abdullah, in which a man of the Emigrants kicked a man of the Ansar and the two war-cries went up. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"What is this call of Jahiliyyah? Abandon it because it is offensive."** Hearing that, Ibn Ubay said, "Have they done so? By Allah, if we return to Al-Madinah, surely, the more honourable will expel therefrom the meaner." 'Umar again rose — "O Allah's Messenger! Let me chop off the head of this hypocrite!" — and the Prophet ﷺ said: **"Leave him, lest the people say that Muhammad kills his companions."** Ibn Kathir notes that Imam Ahmad, Al-Bukhari and Muslim collected this hadith. Jabir's report also records the demographic fact behind the boast: the Ansar were more numerous than the Emigrants when the Messenger ﷺ came to Madinah, though later on the Emigrants increased in number.

## The boast turned back on him

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that Ibn Ubay's words were ambiguous — he named no one — but the intention was clear. By **al-aʿazz**, "the more honourable", he meant himself and the natives of Madinah; by **al-adhall**, "the meanest", he meant — Allah forbid — the Prophet ﷺ and the Emigrant Companions. It was an incitement: he was provoking the Helpers of Madinah against the Emigrants, that they should drive them out of their city.

Allah's reply is one of the most elegant reversals in the Qur'an. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that Allah recoiled his boastful statement back against him: if it is truly the honourable who drive out the truly mean, then the sentence falls on Ibn Ubay himself — because **Al-ʿIzzah belongs to Allah, and to His Messenger, and to the believers.** He named the categories; Allah assigned the names.

**ʿIzzah** is the word at the heart of the passage: might, unassailable honour, the strength that cannot be humbled. Its first belonging is to Allah — this is His, in a manner befitting Him, not the brittle prestige of creatures. It belongs to the Messenger ﷺ and to the believers by Allah's granting, not as something they own in themselves. Which is why it cannot be confiscated by a boycott or by the opinion of the notables of Madinah. Ibn Ubay was a chief with a following, and had none of it. The Emigrants, whom he imagined depended on his people's donations, had all of it.

The story finishes the argument better than any commentary. Ikrimah, Ibn Zayd and others relate that when the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions returned to Madinah, Ibn Ubay's own son 'Abdullah stood at the gate of the city holding his sword. He let the people pass, and when his father came he said, "Stay where you are." His father asked what the matter was, and the son told him he would not be entering through there until the Messenger of Allah allowed him to — "for he is the honourable one and you are the disgraced." (The bundle's wording of that first clause reads, as given, "By Allah! You will enter through here until the Messenger of Allah allows you to do so"; the missing negative appears to be a slip in the text, and the son's own repetition a moment later makes his meaning unmistakable.) When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came up — he used to travel in the last lines — Ibn Ubay complained to him about his son, and the son said, "By Allah, O Allah's Messenger! He will not enter it until you say so." The Messenger ﷺ gave his permission, and only then did the son say, "Enter, now that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave you his permission." The claim of ayah 8 was refuted at the city gate, by the claimant's own child.

In his *Musnad*, Abu Bakr 'Abdullah bin Az-Zubayr Al-Humaydi records from Abu Harun Al-Madani that the son told his father, "You will never enter Al-Madinah unless and until you say, 'Allah's Messenger ﷺ is the honourable one and I am the disgraced'" — and that when the Prophet ﷺ came, the son said to him: I was told you have decided to have my father executed; by Him who has sent you with the Truth, I never looked straight at his face out of respect for him, but if you wish, I will bring you his head myself, because I would hate to see the killer of my father. Look at what faith had done to this family: the father schemed to expel the believers from the city, and the son stood at the gate for the Messenger ﷺ — and the Prophet ﷺ took neither the head nor the revenge.

## "Do not understand" — then "do not know"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to a detail easy to skim past. Ayah 7 ends **lā yafqahūn**, "they do not understand"; ayah 8 ends **lā yaʿlamūn**, "they do not know". Why the change?

Because the two errors are different in kind. If a person thinks that he is the provider of others, Maʿārif says, that is completely irrational — a sign of foolishness, a want of *fiqh*, of depth of comprehension. Honour and dishonour, on the other hand, can fall to anyone's lot; so erring in one's judgement about who has it is ignorance of the facts, of the true state of affairs. So ayah 7 charges them with not understanding, and ayah 8 with not knowing.

## What the passage asks of us

**Never refuse the door while it is open.** Ibn Ubay's ruin was not one bad sentence at a well; it was hearing "come and be prayed for" and turning his head. Repentance offered and declined is heavier than the sin it was offered for.

**Watch for the war-cry.** The Prophet ﷺ called "O Ansar! O Muhajirun!" the call of Jahiliyyah and said to abandon it because it is offensive — and this was between the Emigrants and the Helpers themselves. Any loyalty that can be shouted against another Muslim is the thing this passage came to kill.

**Do not audit your worth by what people can withhold.** Money, position and public standing all belong to the One who owns the treasures of the heavens and the earth. Seek ʿizzah where it actually resides — with Allah, with His Messenger ﷺ, and with the believers — and no one who thinks he is feeding you will ever be able to price you.

passages.title: Wealth, children, and the plea that comes too late
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat close Sūrah al-Munāfiqūn by turning away from the hypocrites and speaking directly to the believers: guard your heart against the two things most likely to pull you away from Allah — your wealth and your children — and spend from what you have *now*, before the moment comes when spending is no longer possible and the only thing left to offer is a plea for more time.

What binds the passage together is a single movement in three steps. Ayah 9 names the danger (distraction). Ayah 10 names the remedy (spending, while you still can) and then, in the same breath, plays back the scene of a man at death asking for exactly the opportunity he is being handed today. Ayah 11 shuts that door: **Allah never delays a soul when its appointed time comes.** The passage is, in effect, an offer with a deadline attached — and the deadline is unknown.

## Why this warning comes here, right after the hypocrites

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the link between the two halves of the sūrah, and it is the key that unlocks the passage. The preceding section dealt with the hypocrites, their false oaths and their conspiracies — and one consequence of that mentality was their design to stop spending on the Emigrant Companions. Strip away the surface and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, their activities were based on one thing: **excessive love for worldly gains.** They outwardly claimed to be Muslims, and might share the spoils of war with the Muslims.

So when Allah now turns and addresses the sincere and faithful believers — *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū* — the warning lands with real force. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it exactly this way: this second section warns the believers against being intoxicated with the love of this world, **as the hypocrites foolishly did.** The same disease that produced their oaths and their stinginess can, in a milder dose, quietly hollow out a believer. This is not a lecture aimed at someone else. It is aimed at the person reciting it.

## "Do not let them divert you" — the precise shape of the prohibition

Notice what ayah 9 does *not* say. It does not say: do not love your wealth. It does not say: do not love your children. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is emphatic on this point — **love of wealth and children to some extent is not bad**; being engaged with them to a certain degree is not only permissible but also obligatory. A man who does not work for his family, or does not care for his children, is not a better Muslim for it.

What the ayah forbids is *diversion*: **lā tulhikum** — as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it, "your riches and your children must not divert you from the remembrance of Allah."

So there is a dividing line between permissible and impermissible love, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the criterion plainly: **this love must not deviate one from Allah's remembrance.** That is the whole test. Not the amount of wealth. Not how much time your children take. Whether the connection to Allah stays intact.

Two things are named — wealth and children — because, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, these are the two major objects in this world that divert a person from the remembrance of Allah, and so they have been named in particular. But the naming is not a limit: otherwise, it refers to all the means of enjoyments in the world. Whatever occupies you the way wealth and children occupy people is included.

## What "the remembrance of Allah" means here

This matters enormously, because the whole verse turns on it. If *dhikr* means only a set of phrases on the tongue, the ayah becomes narrow. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports (citing Qurṭubī) that the word *dhikr* in this context has been variously interpreted by different commentators:

- some said **the five daily prayers**;
- some said **Zakāh**;
- some said **Ḥajj**;
- some said **the Qurʼān**;
- and **Ḥasan al-Baṣrī** expressed the view that it refers to **all forms of obedience and worship**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān judges this last view to be **the most comprehensive interpretation**. On that understanding, ayah 9 is not asking merely whether your wealth makes you miss your adhkār. It is asking whether it makes you cut corners on anything Allah has asked of you: prayer, zakāh, the Qurʼān, every duty owed to Him.

This is a far more searching question than the narrow reading, and far more useful. Most people are not diverted from their religion in one dramatic moment. They are diverted a quarter-hour at a time.

## "Then they are the losers"

The ayah's verdict — *ulāʼika hum al-khāsirūn* — is severe, and both sources dwell on it.

Ibn Kathīr describes those who fall under it as people who engaged in this life, its delights and attributes, and **"were busied from the obedience and remembrance of Allah, for which they were created."** They will be among the losers, and — in his words — they **"will lose themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection."** That is worth pausing over. The very children a man neglected his religion *for* are among what he loses. The thing he sacrificed his ākhirah to secure does not survive the transaction.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the same loss in the language of trade: the verdict applies to the one who becomes engrossed in material wealth or absorbed in the forbidden and abominable things that divert him from his duties towards Allah, because he has **sold the great and eternal reward of the Hereafter for the petty and perishable enjoyment of this world** — and it asks: what loss could be greater than this! A losing trade is not one where you receive nothing; it is one where you receive something worth far less than what you gave up. That is the exact form of this failure. The man who is diverted does get his wealth, and does get his years with his children. He simply pays a price out of all proportion.

## Ayah 10: spend, and spend *now*

Having named the disease, ayah 10 prescribes: **spend out of what We have provided you.** Even the phrasing carries an argument — *min mā razaqnākum*, "out of what **We** have provided you." What you are asked to release was given to you in the first place.

Then the deadline: **before death comes to one of you.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes an important clarification here — "coming of death" in this verse refers to **witnessing the signs of death**, the point at which a person can see it approaching. The verse therefore exhorts believers to make the best of their opportunities to spend in the way of Allah **in the state of good health and strength**, before those signs appear, and so have their degrees of rank elevated in the Hereafter. Once death overtakes them, the opportunity to spend is lost and the wealth will be of no use.

**Why single out spending at all?** If *dhikr* already covers every form of obedience and following the dictates of the Sharīʿah — including spending wealth as due — why does the passage now name spending separately? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two possible reasons, and both are shrewd:

1. **Wealth is the chief obstacle.** One of the major objects that diverts a person from acting upon the sacred law is wealth. Therefore spending wealth — in the form of Zakāh, ʿUshr, Ḥajj and so on — is specifically mentioned, because that is where the resistance lives.
2. **At the end, wealth is the only currency left.** When a person sees the signs of death, it is not in his power to perform his missed prayers, or his missed Ḥajj and Ramaḍān fasts. However, the wealth is right there in front of him, and he is sure that soon it will slip out of his hand. So he may spend it to compensate for his shortfalls in worship and so attain salvation from those shortcomings.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a further encouragement: **charity (ṣadaqah) is efficacious in averting calamities and punishment.** Charity is not only an investment for later; it is a protection now.

## From the Sunnah: the charity that carries the greatest reward

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites here a report recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥs of **Bukhārī and Muslim**, on the authority of **Sayyidunā Abū Hurayrah (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu)**. A person asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Which ṣadaqah attracts most reward?" He ﷺ replied: to spend in Allah's way **while a person is in a state of good health, and yet he fears, in view of future needs, that if he spends the wealth he may become poor.** Then he ﷺ continued: **do not delay spending in Allah's way until such time when your death reaches your throat, and at that moment you instruct your heirs, "give this much to so-and-so and give this much for such and such work."**

That hadith is a perfect commentary on the ayah. It identifies the exact charity the verse is asking for — the difficult one, given while you are strong and still anxious about the future — and it names the exact failure the verse is warning against: the deathbed reallocation of money that is already leaving you anyway.

## The plea — and what stands behind it

The second half of ayah 10 shifts, without warning, into direct speech. The man says: **"My Lord, would You not respite me to a near term — and I will pay ṣadaqah and will become one of the righteous."**

Two details make the plea heartbreaking. First, he does not ask for a long life; he asks for *ajal qarīb*, a **near term**, a little more time. Second, he asks for two things, and in that order: to *give*, and to *become one of the righteous*.

Sayyidunā **Ibn ʿAbbās (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu)** is reported by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān as reading the verse concretely: if **Zakāh was due on a person and he failed to pay it**, and **Ḥajj was obligatory and he failed to perform it**, he will express this desire when death approaches him. He will want a little more time so that he can give ṣadaqah. And "become one of the righteous" carries the rest of it — that he be given a little more time so that he may act righteously by fulfilling the obligations he missed, and repent and ask pardon for the forbidden and abominable acts he might have indulged in.

Ibn Kathīr states it of everyone: **surely, every person who fell into shortcomings will regret it by the time of his death and will ask for respite, even a short period, so that he does better and attains what he missed.** But, he says, no — rather what occurred has occurred and what is coming shall indeed come; each will be held accountable for his mistakes.

Ibn Kathīr then sets this plea beside what Allah says of the disbelievers elsewhere in the Qurʼān. The wrongdoers, on the Day the torment comes upon them, will say: **"Our Lord! Respite us for a little while, we will answer Your call and follow the Messengers!"** — and it will be said to them, *"Had you not sworn aforetime that you would not leave?"* (14:44). And at 23:99–100: until, when death comes to one of them, he says, **"My Lord! Send me back, so that I may do good in that which I have left behind!"** — and the reply is: *No! It is but a word that he speaks; and behind them is Barzakh (a barrier) until the Day when they will be resurrected.*

Ibn Kathīr lets those two passages stand as they are. The Qurʼān's own answer to the request is the whole comment: **"No! It is but a word that he speaks."**

## Ayah 11: the door closes

**"But Allah never delays a soul when its appointed time comes."** Ibn Kathīr's gloss is one sentence, and it needs no more: **when the time of death comes, no one will be granted respite.**

The word for that appointed time is *ajal* — the term fixed for each soul. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the conclusion bluntly: Allah makes it clear in this verse that once a person's time has come, He will not give any more time to anyone, and **this desire at that stage is futile.** Every argument the dying man makes may be sincere — he really would give, he really would reform, a short extension really would be enough. None of it moves the deadline by an instant. The scene in ayah 10 is included precisely so that we hear the plea *while there is still time to make it unnecessary*.

Then the sūrah ends on Allah's name: **wa Allāhu khabīrun bimā taʿmalūn** — "and Allah is All-Aware of what you do."

And notice how much that name is carrying at the end of *this* particular sūrah. It began with the hypocrites, their false oaths and their conspiracies. It ends by telling the believers that Allah is fully aware of what *they* do — their accounts, their giving, their reasons for delay. Nothing here is assessed by appearances.

## Living it

The passage is unusually practical, and its demands are concrete.

**Run the diagnostic in ayah 9 honestly.** Not "do I love money too much?" — almost nobody answers that one truthfully. Ask instead the question the ayah actually poses: *what has my wealth or my family actually caused me to drop?* A prayer at its time. Zakāh paid properly. Time with the Qurʼān. That list is the answer.

**Do not treat provision for your family as a competitor to religion.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that a degree of engagement with wealth and children is not only permissible but obligatory. The problem is never the involvement; it is the involvement that displaces obedience.

**Give while it is inconvenient.** The hadith cited above sets the standard: the ṣadaqah of greatest reward is given in good health, while you still fear poverty. Charity that costs you nothing is not the charity the ayah is pointing at.

**Settle the obligations, not just the optional giving.** Ibn ʿAbbās's reading is a checklist: unpaid Zakāh and unperformed Ḥajj are precisely the debts that surface at the deathbed. Anything you would frantically ask for time to fix then is something you have time to fix now.

**Stop postponing repentance.** The dying man in ayah 10 asks for two things, and the second is to *become one of the righteous*. Both wealth and character are on the same deadline.

The mercy in this passage is easy to miss because of its severity. Allah has shown us in advance, and in the man's own words, exactly what a person will wish for at the end. Everything he begs for is available today to anyone still able to read these lines.
